issues.legal_issue: A High Court is bound by a Supreme Court Constitution Bench’s declared law and cannot decide inconsistently with it.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a High Court judgment that invalidated provisions establishing a land reforms tribunal and transferring certain pending cases.
The High Court treated the relevant directions in an earlier Constitution Bench judgment as not binding law and reached a view inconsistent with those directions.
issues.conclusion: The Constitution Bench’s relevant opinion and directions were law declared under Article 141, binding on the High Court; the inconsistent findings and directions had to be set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 141, law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts. The Court held that the reasoning and directions in paragraphs 98 and 99 of L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) 3 SCC 261 constituted such declared law.

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_decision: A party appealed a High Court decision to a higher court.
predicates.binding_supreme_court_law_applies: An applicable Supreme Court ruling declared a legal principle binding on courts.
predicates.high_court_departed_from_that_law: The High Court adopted a position inconsistent with the applicable Supreme Court ruling.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a High Court decision that departs from applicable declared Supreme Court law, the High Court must follow that law.

issues.legal_issue: A tribunal established to adjudicate disputes under laws concerning land reforms may qualify as a tribunal for land reforms even if the laws are not confined to agrarian reform in a narrow sense.
material_facts: A state law established a tribunal to adjudicate disputes under five specified land-related statutes.

The challengers argued that some of the specified statutes were not concerned with agrarian reform and that the tribunal therefore did not qualify under the constitutional provision for tribunals dealing with land reforms.
The Court considered the statutes’ preambles and schemes and found their objects within the broad concept of land or agrarian reforms.
issues.conclusion: The tribunal qualified as a tribunal under Article 323B; it was not necessary that it deal only with disputes under laws narrowly confined to agrarian reform.
issues.legal_principle: Article 323B(1) and (2)(d) permits tribunals for matters concerning land reforms, and the phrase “or in any other way” is broad. The reference to “estate” in Article 31A serves an enumerative purpose and does not confine Article 323B(2)(d) to agrarian reform narrowly understood. The substance of the legislation, rather than its outward form, is considered. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Mfg. (Wvg.) Co. Ltd. (AIR 1973 SC 2734) for the broad and dynamic understanding of agrarian reform, and considered L. Sampat Kumar and L. Chandra Kumar in discussing tribunals under Article 323B.

predicates.challenge_to_tribunal_status: A party challenged whether a tribunal established by legislation qualifies as a constitutional tribunal for the relevant subject matter.
predicates.tribunal_adjudicates_land_reform_dispute: The tribunal is assigned to decide disputes arising under legislation concerning land reforms.
predicates.legislation_substantively_concerns_land_: The substance and objects of the legislation concern land reforms, even if they are not limited to agrarian reform narrowly understood.

issues.definition: A tribunal challenged on status qualifies when it adjudicates disputes under legislation whose substance concerns land reforms.

issues.legal_issue: A tribunal may act as the court of first instance for assigned disputes, and related exclusions of ordinary court jurisdiction and transfers of pending cases are valid only while constitutional judicial review by the High Court and Supreme Court remains available.
material_facts: The legislation assigned the tribunal first-instance jurisdiction over specified land-related disputes and barred other courts from dealing with those matters, subject to stated exceptions.

The legislation preserved the High Court’s writ jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 when exercised by a Division Bench and excluded pending matters before that Bench from transfer to the tribunal.
The High Court struck down provisions concerning the tribunal’s jurisdiction and transfer of pending matters.
The Supreme Court held that the tribunal could perform a supplemental role as the first forum, with its decisions subject to scrutiny by a Division Bench of the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s findings invalidating the relevant provisions were set aside. The tribunal could act as the first-instance forum, provided its decisions remained subject to High Court review and the constitutional judicial-review jurisdiction was not excluded.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227, High Court judicial review, and under Article 32, Supreme Court judicial review, form part of the Constitution’s basic structure and cannot be ousted. Under L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) 3 SCC 261, tribunals may perform a supplemental role and act as courts of first instance, but their decisions are subject to scrutiny by a Division Bench of the High Court. Article 323B(3)(d) cannot be applied to eliminate that constitutional review.

predicates.challenge_to_tribunal_jurisdiction_or_ca: A party challenges legislation assigning disputes to a tribunal, limiting other courts’ jurisdiction, or transferring pending cases.
predicates.tribunal_is_first_forum_for_assigned_dis: The tribunal is designated to hear the assigned disputes before any High Court review.
predicates.high_court_and_supreme_court_review_rema: The tribunal’s decisions remain open to constitutional review by the High Court and Supreme Court.

issues.definition: A challenged tribunal scheme is valid as a first-instance arrangement when constitutional review of its decisions by the High Court and Supreme Court remains available.
